strengths: Compelling and high-impact application: Bridges high-dimensional 4D atmospheric reanalysis fields with Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to generate structured meteorological warnings and answer domain-specific questions.

Substantial and well-constructed dataset: MP-Bench provides 421,363 aligned pairs over 2,412 stations in China, covering 7 severe weather types plus negative controls, and features diverse task formats across multiple granularities (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW).

Domain-specific architectural design: The three proposed plug-and-play modules (Dynamic Temporal Gating Fusion, Text-Driven Gaussian Spatial Masking, and Text-Driven Channel Attention) effectively address the high dimensionality and spatial/temporal sparsity inherent in 4D gridded atmospheric data.

Promising empirical results and physical consistency: The approach demonstrates clear improvements over multiple open-source MLLM backbones (e.g., +16.1% MC-main accuracy and nearly doubling Macro-F1 on Qwen2.5-VL). Moreover, attention visualizations across pressure levels (e.g., peak attention at 500 hPa for wind dynamics) align well with established synoptic meteorological theory.
weaknesses: Clarification on task setup (Reanalysis vs. Forecasting): The inputs are taken from ERA5 reanalysis over the 12-hour window [t, t+11] following warning issuance at time t. Because ERA5 assimilates actual observations across that time window, this setup corresponds more to automated diagnosis/event identification than true operational forecasting from numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts. The manuscript should explicitly discuss this operational distinction.

Conflation of channel capacity and module contribution in Table 2: The 'Baseline' open-source models in Table 2 are restricted to 3 pressure levels/channels, whereas MMLM utilizes all 185 channels alongside DTGF, TGS, and TGCA. While Table 3 evaluates module ablations on a 5,000-sample subset, the main table lacks a direct baseline that ingests all 185 channels via standard projection to clearly disentangle the benefit of higher vertical resolution from the proposed attention/gating modules.

Heavily reliant on LLM-as-a-judge for NSW: The evaluation for the National Severe Weather (NSW) task relies entirely on GPT-4o scoring on a 0-5 scale. Reporting deterministic extraction metrics (e.g., Precision, Recall, and F1 over predicted <Location, Event, Severity> tuples) would provide a more objective, reproducible assessment.

Minor presentation issues: Incomplete sentences/typos in the text (e.g., 'cores of 1 and 0 are reserved' on page 14, and 'with that the warning' on page 2), and the appendix dedicates excessive space to raw hyperparameter listings (Tables 8 and 9) that could be condensed.

strengths: Introduction of MP-Bench, a large-scale, nationwide multimodal benchmark containing 421,363 samples pairing multi-variable, 4D gridded meteorological fields (ERA5 with 37 vertical pressure levels over 12 hours) with operational severe weather warnings across seven major hazard types.
Well-motivated architectural design (MMLM) tailored to 4D meteorological data, addressing temporal dynamics (DTGF), geographic prompt grounding (TGS), and vertical/variable channel redundancy (TGCA).

Detailed physical consistency analysis in the supplementary material showing that the learned channel and temporal attention distributions align with established meteorological principles (e.g., peak wind weights at 500 hPa, rapid pre-event intensification weights for severe snow/gale warnings).

Extensive experimental evaluation across four major open-source vision-language backbones (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-NeXT-Video, Video-LLaVA, InternVL3) and validation of cross-regional transfer on the US NOAA Storm Events dataset.
weaknesses: Confounding factors between the baseline and proposed MMLM: In Table 2, the baseline models are trained on only 3 meteorological channels/levels, whereas MMLM uses 185 channels along with the proposed modules. It is therefore difficult to isolate how much of the performance leap originates simply from accessing full vertical levels vs. the architectural contributions of DTGF, TGS, and TGCA.

Discrepancy between reanalysis data and real-time early warning: The paper strongly motivates an automated, operational early-warning pipeline, yet uses ERA5 reanalysis over $[t, t+11]$ as inputs. Because ERA5 is a retrospective reanalysis assimilated with post-event observations, this setup evaluates warning extraction from observed atmospheric states rather than true forecasting from real-time NWP forecasts.

Evaluation artifacts with closed-source model: GPT-4o achieves 0.19% accuracy on the binary True/False task (far below the 50% random chance baseline), which strongly suggests an unmitigated output/parsing distribution collapse or extreme response bias rather than a genuine measure of zero-shot reasoning capability.

Evaluation of National Severe Weather (NSW) generation: Relying solely on GPT-4o scoring (on a 0–5 scale, where models score ~1.7–2.1) without reporting standard structured evaluation metrics (e.g., entity/relation precision, recall, and F1 over predicted [location, event, severity] triplets) makes it hard to verify whether the model is hallucinating or missing entities.

strengths: Construction of MP-Bench, a large-scale multimodal benchmark comprising 421,363 pairs connecting multi-level 4D ERA5 meteorological fields with real-world weather warnings from the China Meteorological Administration across 7 severe weather types.
Formulation of diverse downstream question-answering tasks (MC, T/F, Regional RSW, and National NSW) that benchmark MLLMs across different spatial granularities and semantic complexities.

The proposed architecture moves beyond naive 2D RGB compression by integrating domain-tailored modules (DTGF, TGS, and TGCA) to handle temporal variation, spatial focus, and multi-level vertical channels, validated across four modern vision-language backbones.

Detailed qualitative and diagnostic analyses (e.g., in the supplementary material) assessing whether learned channel and temporal attention align with classical synoptic meteorology principles (such as 500 hPa winds and 300 hPa temperature fields).
weaknesses: Conceptual and operational ambiguity regarding 'forecasting': The dataset extracts a 12-hour window [t, t+11] of ERA5 reanalysis data starting at warning issuance time t. ERA5 is a historical reanalysis product incorporating future observational assimilation, not an operational NWP forecast output. In an actual operational early-warning setting, forecasters do not possess future atmospheric reanalysis fields at time t. The task is therefore formulated more as diagnostic/post-hoc verification using future reanalysis rather than true predictive severe weather forecasting.

Unclear and conflicting baseline comparisons: In Table 2, the 'Baseline' model fine-tuned on 3 pressure levels achieves 56.26% MC-main accuracy on Qwen2.5-VL-7B. However, in the ablation study (Table 3), the 185-channel model without any of the three modules (x, x, x) drops to 42.73%. It is unclear whether adding the full 185 vertical channels without the modules causes severe degradation/overfitting, or why the 3-channel baseline strongly outperforms the unmodulated 185-channel setup.

Heuristic nature and brittle assumptions of the proposed modules: TGS relies on parsing exact geographical coordinates directly from the textual prompt via nearest-neighbor coordinate matching to place a static 2D Gaussian mask. This relies heavily on explicit coordinates being provided in the text and does not generalize well to complex spatial descriptions or multiple dispersed affected regions. Similarly, DTGF uses a simple L2 norm between consecutive hours.

Evaluation limitations on the National Severe Weather (NSW) generation task: Performance on NSW is uniformly very low across all models (scores between 0.1 and 2.1 out of 5), indicating limited text-generation capability for nationwide summaries. Furthermore, relying entirely on an uncalibrated LLM-as-a-judge (GPT-4o) without human-expert validation or inter-annotator agreement statistics (such as Cohen's kappa) makes the NSW metrics less reliable.

strengths: High-impact application domain: The paper tackles the challenging problem of bridging raw 4D atmospheric meteorological data (reanalysis grids over time, pressure levels, and space) with natural language severe weather warning generation, moving towards automated meteorological decision support.

Substantial benchmark contribution (MP-Bench): Curating a nationwide, year-round multimodal dataset comprising 421,363 aligned pairs of raw ERA5 data across 37 vertical pressure levels and CMA severe weather warnings across 7 major extreme weather categories provides a valuable benchmark for the community.

Domain-motivated architecture design: The three proposed plug-and-play modules (DTGF for temporal differences, TGCA for cross-layer atmospheric channel re-weighting, and TGS for spatial coordinates) are well-aligned with meteorological domain dynamics and atmospheric physics.

Thorough ablation study: The ablation experiments on 5,000 samples systematically validate each module's individual and cumulative contributions across all evaluation metrics, accompanied by interpretable weight distribution visualizations across pressure heights and lead times.
weaknesses: Task formulation vs. 'Prediction' terminology: The input meteorological data spans a 12-hour window [t, t+11] using ERA5 reanalysis fields after warning issuance time t. Because reanalysis data assimilates actual observations that occurred during [t, t+11], the task is essentially post-hoc diagnosis / event identification rather than purely predictive forecasting based on prior forecast fields. The paper should clearly clarify this distinction to avoid misleading claims of predictive forecasting.

Unfair baseline comparison with GPT-4o: In Table 2, GPT-4o is evaluated zero-shot with heavily compressed 3-channel visual representations, whereas all open-source models are fine-tuned via LoRA on hundreds of thousands of MP-Bench examples with the three specialized modules. Comparing zero-shot generic models against fine-tuned domain-specialized models without making this distinction explicit overstates the relative failure of the closed-source baseline.

Lack of raw open-source base model results in the main benchmark: Table 2 only presents the four open-source models after they are equipped with DTGF, TGS, and TGCA. While Table 3 provides ablations for Qwen2.5-VL-7B on a 5,000 sample subset, reporting the standard baselines (without the proposed modules) across the full test set would provide a clearer baseline comparison.

Presentation and writing typos: Several typos and minor drafting errors exist in the text (e.g., on page 2, 'RSW Questions and RSW Questions' instead of including NSW; 'girddid' on page 5; and equation formatting inconsistencies in Eq. 9).

strengths: The paper addresses an important and emerging problem at the intersection of Earth sciences and multimodal learning: extending multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to ingest complex 4D atmospheric data for severe weather analysis and warning generation.

The introduced MP-Bench dataset is substantial in scale (over 420k pairs) and integrates 12-hour multi-variable 4D ERA5 fields with official warning events across China, spanning 7 severe weather types and multiple QA formats (MC, T/F, RSW, NSW).

The architectural design introduces sensible domain-tailored modules (DTGF for temporal differences, TGS for spatial conditioning, and TGCA for multi-level atmospheric channel selection), avoiding the crude temporal/vertical collapsing common in standard vision encoders.

Comprehensive empirical evaluations are conducted across four recent MLLM backbones (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Video-LLaVA, and LLaVA-NeXT) along with ablation studies validating the individual contributions of the three proposed modules.
weaknesses: Task formulation vs. Forecasting reality: The paper claims to address 'severe weather event prediction/forecasting', but the input data consists of ERA5 reanalysis fields extracted over the 12-hour window [t, t+11] after the warning issuance time t. ERA5 is an atmospheric reanalysis produced post-hoc using data assimilation of actual observations. Using reanalysis data occurring during the event is diagnosis/nowcasting, not true forecasting, because in real-time operational deployment at time t, ERA5 for [t, t+11] is unavailable (only NWP forecasts exist).

Potential leakage or ambiguous wording in TGS: In Section 'TGS', the text states: 'M(u, v) represents the sum of Gaussian weight masks corresponding to all coordinates extracted from the text-based weather warnings.' If the coordinates are extracted from the ground-truth weather warnings rather than purely from the user query/prompt, this would introduce severe target leakage. If this was intended to refer to query coordinates, it needs explicit clarification, especially regarding how TGS operates during national-scale queries (NSW) where target event coordinates are unknown beforehand.

Unfair baseline comparison with GPT-4o: In Table 2, GPT-4o is evaluated in a zero-shot setting on a 3-channel 2D projection, whereas open-source models are fine-tuned via LoRA on hundreds of thousands of domain-specific 4D samples with dedicated adapters. While this demonstrates the limitation of off-the-shelf vision models, presenting it as a primary baseline comparison without clearly highlighting the disparate fine-tuning and input modalities is somewhat misleading.

Experimental inconsistencies and clarity issues: (1) In Table 2, Qwen2.5-VL with all modules achieves 72.37% on MC-main, whereas in Table 3 (ablation), Qwen2.5-VL with all modules achieves 57.23%. The text notes 5,000 instances were sampled for ablation, but it is ambiguous whether this was a smaller fine-tuning set or an evaluation subset. (2) On the national-scale task (NSW), all models achieve scores below 2.1 out of 5, indicating that generation of multi-event national summaries remains largely unsolved, yet qualitative inspection and error analysis of this failure mode are limited.

Noticeable typographical and presentation errors: On page 2, the text states 'four types of QA pairs, including Multiple Choice Questions, True/False Questions, RSW Questions and RSW Questions' (repeating RSW instead of NSW); Equation (9) contains a formatting artifact ('P¦' instead of P^T); and Table 1 in the Appendix is misreferenced as Table 2.

strengths: Large-scale multimodal meteorological dataset: MP-Bench compiles over 420k instances combining multi-level ERA5 gridded reanalysis data with official CMA severe weather warnings across China, establishing a diverse benchmark encompassing multiple QA formats (MC, T/F, regional, and nationwide queries).

Preservation of vertical atmospheric structure: Rather than collapsing atmospheric variables into 2D surface fields, the work incorporates 37 pressure levels across multiple variables (185 channels) and explores dedicated module designs (TGCA, DTGF, TGS) to handle multi-dimensional meteorological inputs.

Component ablations: The authors provide an ablation study isolating the contributions of the temporal gating (DTGF), spatial masking (TGS), and channel attention (TGCA) modules, supported by qualitative weight distribution visualizations.
weaknesses: Flawed forecasting formulation and temporal leakage: The paper positions itself as early-warning severe weather prediction, yet Section 'Data Alignment' states that the model ingests ERA5 reanalysis data spanning [t, t+11] hours starting at the warning issuance time t. In an operational forecasting setting, ERA5 reanalysis of future hours is unavailable (only NWP forecast forecasts or antecedent observations are available). Ingesting concurrent/future ground-truth reanalysis fields makes the task diagnostic hindcasting/event detection rather than predictive forecasting.

Severely compromised and flawed baseline comparison: In Table 2, closed-source GPT-4o is reported with a 0.19% accuracy on binary True/False questions. For a two-alternative forced-choice task where random guess yields ~50%, a score of 0.19% strongly indicates a format failure, output parsing error, or completely mismatched prompting rather than meaningful task performance. Comparing a heavily fine-tuned model (LoRA on 220k samples with 185 channels) against an unadapted, zero-shot GPT-4o fed arbitrary 3-channel composite images is unconvincing and unfair.

Lack of standard open-source baselines without proposed modules: In Table 2, all reported open-source models are already augmented with the proposed modules. The standalone performance of the unmodified open-source base models across the full test set is omitted from the main benchmark table, making it difficult to decouple the intrinsic capability of modern MLLMs from the benefits of the proposed modules.

Heuristic module designs and missing architecture details: The proposed modules rely largely on simple heuristics (e.g., TGS is a static 2D Gaussian mask centered on coordinates parsed from the prompt, which fails or is undefined for non-localized tasks like NSW). Furthermore, the exact architectural mechanism for mapping the 4D input tensor (time, 185 channels, height, width) through the 3D convolution and projection layer into the respective MLLM visual token spaces lacks formal specification and dimensional bookkeeping.

Severe performance failure on complex tasks and minority classes: Nationwide generation (NSW) achieves only 1.7–2.1 out of 5 across all models, and snowstorm accuracy falls below 6% (Fig. 5) due to severe class imbalance. The paper provides no algorithmic solutions or loss weighting to handle this prominent extreme-event tail distribution.

Editorial and typographical oversights: The manuscript contains multiple errors, such as repeating 'RSW Questions and RSW Questions' on page 2, typos like 'girdded' / 'griddid' (pages 4 and 5), 'f6%' instead of '<6%' (page 6), and punctuation/spacing issues throughout.
